en: Overcame the great men whose fame he heard.
They wore coats no bullet could pierce.
Infidel or Muslim,
They attacked whoever bore them malice.
Those who heard the news cried out.
Hearing your father's name,
Even the khan of Beijing wept.
No giant came to challenge him.
That handful of Kyrgyz,
While your khan father lived,
Did not ask the father,
Khan Manas the Leopard died;
Your tiger Bakai died while alive;
All the people died.
When my wolf-maned Manas died,
When this head of mine suffered humiliation,
Your grandfather Zhakyp, the foolish khan,
A Muslim like Azazil himself,
Loving discord, began to speak.
The peoples of three khans clashed.
When your father Manas died,
Before forty days had passed,
Roaring in anger,
He summoned Bagdoolot's six sons.
He spoke murderous words of discord,
Spoke of a time when the people would perish.
Roaring in anger,
He summoned his six wicked ones,
And wished for turmoil in this way.
Let me tell you of your grandfather, the swine khan.
Then he stirred up his six wicked ones:
“When a horse dies, a great dog
Has need of its rump.
When an elder brother dies, you six wicked ones,
You have need of your sister-in-law.
When that Manas died,
You settled along the valley,
You desperate kinsmen, six wicked ones,
And became like a fire gone out.
When Manas died, you all died;
All of you worthless, six wicked ones,
Losing your worth, you died again.
I heard news from those who came:
Your ill-fated sister-in-law—
Six thousand ingots and a thousand otters
Bakai has swallowed as a bribe,
And to Ormombek of the goat-herders
I heard he will help her escape.”
Thus he wished for turmoil,
Setting his worthless sons upon her,
Your grandfather, the swine khan, urged them on.
From that scoundrel came strife;
The forty companions began the fighting.
Your grandfather, the swine khan, stirred up the quarrel.
When they devised their wicked plan,
You were a young boy in her arms.
My dear child Kanykei—
The dogs burst in and trampled her,
Struck her breast and split it open.
When your mother suffered humiliation,
When your mountain-like father died,
When his countless treasures were scattered,
You were pulled from the cradle;
Your grandmother Chyiyrdy carried you away.
A black bondwoman's child
Your mother swaddled in the cradle,
And nursed intently.
The six wicked ones came straight in,
When they had worked out their plan.
The six wicked ones swung their battle-axes,
And struck down my precious child Kanykei.
“This is Semetey,” they said.
The black bondwoman's child in the cradle,
With Arkesken, the six wicked ones
Struck into two pieces.
When their enmity was known for certain,
To Temir Khan's city,
When your mother wandered,
To Kara Khan's city,
When your mother fled,
“Go and reach Temir Khan,” I said.
I, Bakai, caught up behind her,
Gave two skins of milk,
Gave two fat horses,
They slaughtered the gray wether now.
I stood lamenting, my orphan,
Entrusting you to Kanykei.
Sending you over Zhorgonun-Zholu,
I made you disappear,
Helping you flee this Talas.
I did not die, my orphan.
If I wished to die, life was sweet;
If I wished to enter it, the earth was hard.
Abyke and Kobosh, the six wicked ones,
Your precious uncle Bakai
Would never leave in peace.
At the marsh of Uyrulmo,
They gathered round in assembly.
At the marsh of Chogulma,
They plotted great mischief.
Tekechi Khan, Shygai Khan,
And Zhamgyrchy of the Eshtek—
The peoples of three khans gathered
“This is Bakai who helped the shameless woman flee,”
They said, laying charges against poor me.
They drew bows and shot like rain,
Fired bullets thicker than hail.
When the dogs came to surround me,
I struck my gray steed once,
Took my blue musket in hand,
And stayed without growing weary.
For many days and many nights,
I exchanged fire without rest.
Breaking down roads, holding a fortress,
Holding an impregnable position,
I, Bakai, endured suffering.
Skilled as I was, dear soul,
Of that wicked Abyke's men
I shot sixty warriors.
I camped up along the dark cliff.
My dear child, on your account,
I became the subject of an outcry.
And, my son, listen:
I acquired a bad name.
My precious one, on your account,
I stayed without growing weary.
With those wicked ones, I myself
Exchanged fire for twelve years.
I spent long days herding camels,
Wondering whether my dear child left by Lord Manas
Would ever come.
I spent long days herding livestock,
Wondering whether my orphan left by the hero
Would ever come.
Orphan, wait here a moment.
The reason you must wait—
A pit has been dug for you;
Misfortune is brewing for you.
Upon your head, my only one,
A strange and painful ordeal awaits.
This Talas is no land for you.
Why should I tell the rest?
Your grandfather, the swine khan, is no kin to you!
He will begin mischief against you,
Will show you, my foal,
Wonders no human would devise.
My orphan, if he lives, you will see.
There will be evasiveness in his words,
Ill intent in his eyes,
If he can, he means to slaughter you.
There will be guile in his words,
Mischief in his eyes.
If the swine khan acts first,
He will seek to slaughter you.
In your grandfather the swine's house
There is bozo in a leather bucket,
With burning poison mixed into it.
There is bozo in a wooden tub,
Potent poison was mixed as well.
A bearskin and a great carpet—
Do not sit alone upon that finery.
Beneath it, dug in readiness,
Is a pit forty fathoms deep.
If you sit there, my child,
Your leopard Khan Bakai must answer for it.
If you knowingly refuse my words,
Your uncle Bakai will suffer misfortune.
I have told you of the suffering; understand.
Without killing me, orphan, heed my words.
My cherished treasure left by Manas,
Turn your horse's head aside,
My orphan, wait at the place ahead.
That looming shape you see,
The inheritance left by your father Manas,
Almambet and Chubak's
Royal camp set up as a watchpost—
If you ask what it is now,
It is your grandfather the swine khan's camp.
Let me go to your grandfather, the swine khan.
He is your father's father;
For the spirit's sake, for the patron's sake,
Let me greet him.
“Your orphan left by the precious one
Has now arrived,” I shall say.
If your swine khan is honorable,
Let me take the reward for good news.
If your khan grandfather is wicked,
Let me bring turmoil and trouble upon him.
Let me grapple with the dog,
And take my long-standing revenge upon him.
If your grandfather is honest,
Let me test his conduct.
If he is wicked, let me
Plunder the fool's fine cloth,
And unleash great turmoil.
Let me enter his royal camp,
Between wickedness and honesty
Draw a boundary and find out.
Turn your horse's head aside,
My supporting kinsman, found late in life,
Wait at the place ahead.
If I lose you, it will be a disgrace.
My orphan, I entrust you to the one God!”
So saying, mighty Bakai
Left the boy there.
He struck his gray steed once,
Beat the drum once,
And raced toward the grandfather, the swine khan.
Wrenched away from the entrance.
At Khan Zhakyp's tethering rail
He tied up Kokcholok.
Into Khan Zhakyp's royal camp
Bakai, standing boldly,
Offering greetings, unflinching,
Now entered again:
“Peace and greetings, peace be upon you,
My renowned elder, the khan,
Are your illustrious people well?
We fought for twelve years.
Khan Zhakyp, consider: this year we meet again.
We wore bloodstained clothing.
When Manas died, everyone died;
We struggled worse than with the Chinese.
When did we ever observe proper custom?
Foolishly becoming the subject of gossip,
Old man, we went without meeting.
Here is Keng-Kol, here is the land.
If you mean to cut off my head,
Here I am, the same old Bakai!
Here are the Kyrgyz people with their towns.
My dear elder, if you mean to spill my blood, here I am!”
So saying, Khan Bakai
Boldly offered his greeting,
And Sultan Bakai entered.
When his eyes saw Bakai,
The grandfather, the swine khan—
God struck him utterly astray!
Bakai greeted him; there was no reply.
He turned about, drawing himself up,
Looked away, hunching down.
Grasping his battle-ax, he growled,
As though ready to start mischief at once.
He turned away, trembling.
Sidling as though rabid,
The grandfather, the swine khan,
Started a quarrel as soon as he saw Khan Bakai:
“Accustomed to stirring up discord,
Is that you, Bakai, you swine?
Killing sixty of dear Abyke's warriors,
Did you know you could not die?
Bakai, you slave, did you think you would not die?
Did you know you could not diminish?
Bakai, did you think you would never depart?
Bakai, you killed a camel; a claim lies against you.
Have you come, bloodthirsty Bakai?
You who struck down sixty warriors,
